subject: Music
examFormat: Three papers, all compulsory. Paper 1 is a 1-hour objective test of forty multiple-choice questions for 40 marks. Paper 2 is a 2-hour essay paper with five questions, of which three are answered, for 60 marks; Question 1 (Theory/Composition) and Question 2 (analysis of prescribed set-works) are compulsory. Paper 3A is a 45-minute aural test for 50 marks and Paper 3B a 30-minute performance test for 50 marks, on an instrument of choice including voice.
excluded: Ghana-only material (Ghanaian traditional, popular and art musicians; Ghanaian dances; Ghana performance lists), the yearly prescribed set-works (2013-2017), the performance-test piece lists and the supervisors' conduct notes were left out as Ghana-specific, set-text or administrative. The performance appendix of technical exercises was only summarised.

subtopics.name: Modes (African)

subtopics.name: Transcription

subtopics.name: Musical terms, signs, ornaments and abbreviations
Chords/Triads

Identify secondary chords (ii, iii, vi) and their inversions

subtopics.name: Chord Progressions and Cadences
objectives: Identify cadences in major and minor keys: perfect (V-I), plagal (IV-I), interrupted (V-vi) and imperfect (I-V, ii-V, iii-V, IV-V)

objectives: Continue a given melodic phrase in a major or minor key to form a melody of not less than 12 and not more than 16 bars, modulating to at least one specified related key where required

subtopics.name: Setting a text to music

subtopics.name: Simple forms
objectives: Identify simple forms, e.g. binary, ternary, rondo

subtopics.name: Extended forms
objectives: Identify extended forms, e.g. overture, oratorio, opera, cantata, suite, sonata, symphony, concerto

subtopics.name: Form in traditional African music
objectives: Identify forms in traditional African music: antiphony (call and response, cantor/chorus, call and refrain) and repetitive (cyclic) forms

subtopics.name: Form in contemporary African art music
objectives: Analyse form in contemporary African art music with emphasis on compositional techniques, e.g. use of melody, rhythm, harmony, instrumentation and through-composed pieces

subtopics.name: Prepared set-works
objectives: Study the prescribed set-works (Western or African) for the compulsory analysis question in Paper 2

topics.name: Aural Tests (Paper 3A)
topics.content: Candidates write all seven tests, administered by recording. (a) Rhythmic dictation: a melody not exceeding 4 bars, played four times; candidates write the rhythm on a monotone, in simple or compound time (8 marks). (b) Melody writing: from dictation, a short melodic passage not exceeding 4 bars, possibly with elements of African music, modal or in a major/minor key (8 marks). (c) Writing the upper or lower part of a two-part phrase of not more than four bars in a major or minor key (8 marks). (d) Chords: identify the chords (not more than eight) in a progression in a named key using Roman numerals or a technical description (8 marks). (e) Cadences: recognise and name perfect, imperfect, interrupted or plagal cadences in a major key; four examples (6 marks). (f) Modulations: recognise and name simple changes of key to the dominant, subdominant, and relative major or minor; four examples (6 marks). (g) Identification/description of themes: identify or describe three themes or excerpts, at least one African, limited to form, style or genre, principal instrument(s), scale or mode and meter (6 marks).

topics.name: Performance Test (Paper 3B)
topics.content: Every candidate offers an instrument or voice for a practical examination, including sight-reading (two sight-reading tests, simple or compound time) and technical exercises, scales and arpeggios. Approved instruments: voice; pianoforte/electronic keyboard; violin and guitar; recorder (descant and treble), atenteben, flute, clarinet, saxophone, trumpet, trombone, euphonium and tuba. Candidates perform pieces from the approved list only; the test lasts about 30 minutes. The marking schedule is 50 marks: technical exercises/scales 10, one piece from list A 15, one piece from list B 15, sight reading 10.

topics.name: History and Literature of Music: Nigerian Traditional Musicians
objectives: Show general knowledge of Nigerian traditional musicians/composers
topics.content: Examples named: Ezigbo Obiligbo, Dan Maraya, Haruna Ishola, Ayinla Omowura, Dauda Epoakara, Odolaye Aremu, Ogundare Foyanmu, Hubert Ogunde, Israel Nwoba, Mamman Shata, etc. Only a general (non-specialist) knowledge of the composers, periods, works and forms is expected.

topics.name: History and Literature of Music: Nigerian Popular Musicians
objectives: Show general knowledge of Nigerian popular musicians by genre
topics.content: Highlife: Victor Olaiya, Celestine Ukwu, Inyang Henshaw, Zeal Onyia, Victor Uwaifor, Nico Mbarga, Roy Chicago, Rex Jim Lawson, Bobby Benson, Stephen Osita Osadebey, Eddie Okonta, Adeolu Akinsanya. Afrobeat: Fela Anikulapo Kuti, Femi Kuti, Orlando Julius Ekemode. Juju: I. K. Dairo, Fatai Rolling Dollar, Ebenezer Obey, Sunny Ade, Prince Adekunle, Segun Adewale, Dele Abiodun, Shina Peters. Fuji: Sikiru Ayinde Barrister, Ayinla Kollington, Rasheed Ayinde, Wasiu Ayinde Marshall, Abass Obesere, Wasiu Alabi Pasuma, Saheed Osupa. Waka: Batile Alake, Kuburatu Alaragbo, Salawatu Abeni. Afro-Pop: Onyeka Onwenu, Christy Essien Igbokwe, Sonny Okosuns, Mike Okri, Chris Okotie, Bisade Ologunde (Lagbaja), Zaki Adze. Afro-Reggae: Terra Kota, Majek Fashek, Ras Kimono, Victor Essiet, Evi Edna-Ogholi. Hip-Hop: Tuface Idibia, Dbanj, P-Square, Paul Dairo, 9ice, Wande Coal, Terry Gee, Davido, etc.

topics.name: History and Literature of Music: Contemporary Nigerian Art Musicians
objectives: Show general knowledge of contemporary Nigerian art musicians
topics.content: T. K. E. Phillips, Fela Sowande, Ayo Bankole, W.W.C. Echezona, Adam Fiberesima, Dayo Dedeke, Akin Euba, Sam Akpabot, Ikoli Harcourt-Whyte, Laz Ekwueme, Okechukwu Ndubuisi, Sam Ojukwu, Bode Omojola, Ayo Oluranti, Debo Akinwunmi, Christian Onyeji, Richard Okafor.

topics.name: History and Literature of Western Music
objectives: Show general knowledge of Western composers by period
topics.content: Medieval (ca. 450-1400): Guillaume de Machaut, Johannes Ockeghem, Jacob Obrecht. Renaissance (ca. 1400-1600): Guillaume Dufay, Thomas Tallis, John Cooke, John Tudor, Josquin des Prez, Orlando di Lasso, John Dowland, Orlando Gibbons, William Byrd, John Dunstable, Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina. Baroque (ca. 1600-1750): Claudio Monteverdi, Antonio Vivaldi, Arcangelo Corelli, Henry Purcell, Johann Sebastian Bach, George Frideric Handel, Domenico Scarlatti. Classical (ca. 1750-1820): Willibald Gluck, Josef Haydn, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Jan Ladislav Dussek, Muzio Clementi, C.P.E. Bach, Ludwig van Beethoven. Romantic (ca. 1820-1900): Franz Schubert, Robert Schumann, Clara Schumann, Felix Mendelssohn, Frederic Chopin, Franz Liszt, Johannes Brahms, Hector Berlioz, Richard Wagner, Antonin Dvorak, Claude Debussy, Maurice Ravel, Johann Strauss, P. I. Tchaikovsky, the Russian Five (Mussorgsky, Balakirev, Cui, Borodin and Rimsky-Korsakov). 20th century (ca. 1900-2000): Bela Bartok, Igor Stravinsky, Arnold Schoenberg, Paul Hindemith, Aaron Copland, Heitor Villa-Lobos, Saint-Saens.

topics.name: Black Music in the Diaspora
objectives: Show general knowledge of Black musicians and forms in the Diaspora
topics.content: Musicians: Scott Joplin, Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith, Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, John Coltrane, Aretha Franklin, Miles Davis, James Brown, Diana Ross, Lord Kitchener, Mighty Sparrow, Jimmy Cliff, Bob Marley, Michael Jackson, Hugh Masekela, Miriam Makeba. Forms: Spiritual, Jazz, Blues, Rock, Gospel, Soul, Calypso, Reggae and Afrobeat. Questions may also be asked on current and very widely known musicians of African origin.

topics.name: Traditional and Contemporary African Music
topics.content: Nigerian dances to be studied: Bata, Egwu Amala, Atilogwu, Swange, Apiiri, etc.
